best_facts.fact: Convicted in 399 BCE, Socrates was invited to propose his own penalty and first suggested free meals for life at public expense, the honour given to Olympic champions.
best_facts.why_surprising: A man on trial for his life asked for a reward.

best_facts.fact: Teachers' Day in India, 5 September, is the birthday of a philosopher: Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, who asked students in 1962 to honour all teachers instead of him.
best_facts.why_surprising: Every teacher's card in India honours a philosophy professor.

best_facts.fact: Edmund Gettier's 1963 paper is three pages long, was reportedly written to secure tenure, and was essentially his only publication in epistemology. It still generates new papers six decades later.

Aristotle says Thales, mocked for being poor, predicted a big olive harvest, hired every olive press in Miletus in advance and made a fortune renting them out, to prove philosophers could be rich if they wanted.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first recorded options trade was a philosopher's point of honour.

best_facts.fact: Ludwig Wittgenstein thought his first book had solved philosophy, so he gave away one of Europe's largest fortunes and became a village schoolteacher in Austria.
best_facts.why_surprising: Solving philosophy was, for him, a reason to quit it.

best_facts.fact: The word 'scientist' did not exist until William Whewell coined it in the 1830s; before that, physicists like Newton were natural philosophers, and his 1687 masterpiece calls itself natural philosophy.
best_facts.why_surprising: Science is younger, as a word, than the railway.

best_facts.fact: The Rig Veda's Nasadiya hymn ends its account of creation by saying that the one who watches from the highest heaven may know how it began, or perhaps does not know.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the world's oldest scriptures ends in honest doubt.

best_facts.fact: Frank Jackson's Mary's room argument against physicalism became famous, and then Jackson himself changed his mind and became a physicalist.
best_facts.why_surprising: A classic argument outlived its author's belief in it.

best_facts.fact: Marcus Aurelius's bronze horse statue survived the Middle Ages, when most pagan bronzes were melted, probably because people thought it showed the Christian emperor Constantine.
best_facts.why_surprising: A case of mistaken identity saved the philosopher-emperor.

best_facts.fact: When James Stockdale was shot down over North Vietnam in 1965, he thought, as he parachuted, that he was leaving the world of technology and entering the world of Epictetus. He was held for seven and a half years.
Ambedkar's most famous essay, Annihilation of Caste, is a speech he was never allowed to give: the 1936 Lahore organisers asked for cuts, he refused, and printed it himself.
best_facts.why_surprising: A cancelled speech became a classic.

best_facts.fact: Descartes first wrote 'I think, therefore I am' in French in 1637; the Latin 'cogito, ergo sum' came seven years later, and his Meditations does not use the familiar formula at all.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most famous Latin line in philosophy began in French.

best_facts.fact: Ibn Sina's 'floating man', imagined in the early 11th century, argued that a person suspended in empty air with no sensations would still know he exists, six centuries before Descartes.
best_facts.why_surprising: The cogito had a Persian ancestor.

best_facts.fact: In 1936 Alan Turing invented the abstract design of the modern computer in order to answer a question about logic posed by David Hilbert.
best_facts.why_surprising: The computer was a by-product of a philosophical puzzle.

best_facts.fact: Mary Midgley published her first book at 59 and kept writing philosophy into her late nineties.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of Britain's best-known philosophers started late.

best_facts.fact: Kant published the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781, at 57, after about a decade in which he published almost nothing.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the most important books in philosophy came from a late bloomer.

best_facts.fact: A 2015 UK trial of Philosophy for Children with over 3,000 pupils reported gains, but a larger trial reported in 2021 found little effect on attainment.
best_facts.why_surprising: Philosophy's own claims get tested like medicine.

best_facts.fact: MIT's Moral Machine collected about 40 million decisions from 233 countries and territories about how self-driving cars should resolve trolley-style dilemmas.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 1967 seminar puzzle became a global data set.

side_dish.title: The brain that asks why: wonder in the lab
side_dish.body_md:
Plato and Aristotle said philosophy begins in **wonder**. Neuroscience has started to measure something close to it: **curiosity**.

In a 2009 study at Caltech, Min Jeong Kang, Colin Camerer and colleagues put volunteers in a brain scanner and showed them trivia questions, such as *what instrument was invented to sound like a human singing?* People rated how curious they were before the answer appeared. Higher curiosity went with stronger activity in the **caudate**, a region tied to anticipating rewards, and people remembered surprising answers better.

In 2014, Matthias Gruber and colleagues at UC Davis found a bonus effect. When people were in a curious state, they also remembered **unrelated faces** shown during the wait better, and the effect was linked to the brain's dopamine circuits and the hippocampus, the memory hub. Curiosity seems to put the brain into a learning mode that spills over onto whatever comes next.

This gives a modern twist to Russell's claim that philosophy is valuable for its questions. A good open question is not a failure to know. It is a state the brain treats as a reward in itself, and one that makes you better at learning everything around it. That is also why Daily Atlas asks you to guess before you read: a prequestion opens the gap that curiosity wants to close.

offline_task.title: Run one Socratic conversation
offline_task.body_md:
Today, have one ten-minute conversation the way Socrates did. You need one willing friend, colleague or family member.

1. Ask them for a confident claim they hold about a big word: *a good design is...*, *a fair boss is...*, *a real friend is...*.
2. Ask what they mean. Write their definition down.
3. Look together for one counterexample: a case that fits the definition but obviously is not the thing, or is the thing but does not fit. Remember Diogenes's chicken.
4. Improve the definition. Repeat once or twice.
5. Stop while it is still friendly. The goal is not to win but to see more clearly, which is what Nyaya called *vada*, as opposed to *jalpa*.

Tonight, write two lines: the definition you started with, and the one you ended with. If they are different, you have done philosophy.
